scenes.title: Cron & Job Scheduling
scenes.narration: Cron is the classic Unix scheduler that runs your scripts automatically at set times, making it a backbone of data pipelines.

scenes.title: Why Scheduling Matters
bullets: Data pipelines often need to run nightly, hourly, or on a fixed rhythm.
Cron removes the human from routine jobs so they never get forgotten.
You edit your schedule through a per-user file called the crontab.
scenes.narration: Most data work is recurring, whether it is a nightly load or an hourly refresh, and that regularity is exactly what a scheduler handles. Cron takes the person out of the loop, so a job fires reliably even at three in the morning. You manage all of this through your crontab, a simple per-user list of scheduled commands.

scenes.title: Reading a Cron Schedule
scenes.narration: A cron schedule is five fields separated by spaces, standing for minute, hour, day of month, month, and day of week. An asterisk in any field means every value. Reading them in order turns a cryptic string into a plain-English time.

scenes.title: Scheduling a Job
scenes.code:
crontab -e     # edit your schedule

# run the ETL every day at 2:30 AM
30 2 * * * /usr/bin/python3 /home/data/etl.py >> /var/log/etl.log 2>&1

# run every 15 minutes
*/15 * * * * /home/data/check.sh
scenes.narration: You open your schedule with crontab -e. The first job's five fields read as thirty minutes past two, every day, so it runs the ETL nightly, redirecting both output and errors into a log file. The second line uses the slash syntax to fire every fifteen minutes. Always use full absolute paths, because cron runs with a minimal environment.

scenes.text: Cron has a bare environment and no PATH, so use absolute paths and redirect output to a log — silent failures are the top cron pitfall.
scenes.narration: Cron runs with almost no environment, so relative paths and assumed variables often break jobs quietly. Use absolute paths and capture output to a log so failures never go unnoticed.
